summary: `tokio::io::ReadHalf<T>::unsplit` is Unsound
details:
`tokio::io::ReadHalf<T>::unsplit` can violate the `Pin` contract

The soundness issue is described in the [tokio/issues#5372](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/issues/5372)

Specific set of conditions needed to trigger an issue (a !Unpin type in ReadHalf)
is unusual, combined with the difficulty of making any arbitrary use-after-free
exploitable in Rust without doing a lot of careful alignment of data types in
the surrounding code.

The `tokio` feature `io-util` is also required to be enabled to trigger this
soundness issue.

Thanks to zachs18 reporting the issue to Tokio team responsibly and taiki-e
and carllerche appropriately responding and fixing the soundness bug.

Tokio before 0.2.0 used `futures` 0.1 that did not have `Pin`, so it is not
affected by this issue.

summary: atty potential unaligned read
details:
On windows, `atty` dereferences a potentially unaligned pointer.

In practice however, the pointer won't be unaligned unless a custom global allocator is used.

In particular, the `System` allocator on windows uses `HeapAlloc`, which guarantees a large enough alignment.

# atty is Unmaintained

A Pull Request with a fix has been provided over a year ago but the maintainer seems to be unreachable.

Last release of `atty` was almost 3 years ago.

## Possible Alternative(s)

The below list has not been vetted in any way and may or may not contain alternatives;

- [std::io::IsTerminal](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/io/trait.IsTerminal.html) - Stable since Rust 1.70.0
- [is-terminal](https://crates.io/crates/is-terminal) - Standalone crate supporting Rust older than 1.70.0"

summary: Race Condition Enabling Link Following and Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition in remove_dir_all
details:
The `remove_dir_all` crate is a Rust library that offers additional features over the Rust standard library `fs::remove_dir_all` function. It suffers the same class of failure as the code it was layering over: TOCTOU race conditions, with the ability to cause arbitrary paths to be deleted by substituting a symlink for a path after the type of the path was checked.

Thanks to the Rust security team for identifying the problem and alerting us to it.

summary: Shaman has soundness issues and is unmaintained
details:
`shaman::cryptoutil::write_u64v_le` and other functions mentioned above cannot garantee memory safety of get_unchecked later if both length are zero.

`shaman` is unmaintained.

summary: anon-vec lacks sufficient checks in public API
details:
The following functions in the anon-vec crate are unsound due to insufficient checks on their arguments::

- `AnonVec::get_ref()`
- `AnonVec::get_mut()`
- `AnonVec::remove_get()`

The crate was built as a learning project and is not being maintained.

summary: xous has unsound usages of `core::slice::from_raw_parts`
details:
We consider `as_slice` and `as_slice_mut` unsound because: the pointer with any bit patterns could be cast to the slice of arbitrary types. The pointer could be created by unsafe new and deprecated `from_parts`. We consider that `from_parts` should be removed in latest version because it will help trigger unsoundness in `as_slice`. With new declared as unsafe, `as_slice` should also declared as unsafe.  

This was patched in by marking two functions as `unsafe`.

summary: magic-crypt uses insecure cryptographic algorithms
details:
This crate uses a number of cryptographic algorithms that are no longer considered secure and it uses them in ways that do not guarantee the integrity of the encrypted data.

`MagicCrypt64` uses the insecure DES block cipher in CBC mode without authentication. This allows for practical brute force and padding oracle attacks and does not protect the integrity of the encrypted data. Key and IV are generated from user input using CRC64, which is not at all a key derivation function.

`MagicCrypt64`, `MagicCrypt128`, `MagicCrypt192`, and `MagicCrypt256` are all vulnerable to padding-oracle attacks. None of them protect the integrity of the ciphertext. Furthermore, none use password-based key derivation functions, even though the key is intended to be generated from a password.

Each of the implementations are unsound in that they use uninitialized memory without `MaybeUninit` or equivalent structures.

For more information, visit the [issue](https://github.com/magiclen/rust-magiccrypt/issues/17).

summary: linkme fails to ensure slice elements match the slice's declared type
details:
Affected versions allow populating a DistributedSlice of T with elements of an arbitrary other type that coerces to T. For example, elements of type `&&str` could end up in a slice of type `[&str]`, since `&&str` coerces to `&str` via a deref coercion.

The flaw was corrected by implementing typechecking for distributed slice elements in such a way that coercion no longer occurs. The element's type must be a subtype of the slice's declared element type.

summary: XMP Toolkit's `XmpFile::close` can trigger undefined behavior
details:
Affected versions of the crate failed to catch C++ exceptions raised within the `XmpFile::close` function. If such an exception occurred, it would trigger undefined behavior, typically a process abort.

This is best demonstrated in [issue #230](https://github.com/adobe/xmp-toolkit-rs/issues/230), where a race condition causes the `close` call to fail due to file I/O errors.

This was fixed in [PR #232](https://github.com/adobe/xmp-toolkit-rs/pull/232) (released as crate version 1.9.0), which now safely handles the exception.

For backward compatibility, the existing API ignores the error. A new API `XmpFile::try_close` was added to allow callers to receive and process the error result.

Users of all prior versions of `xmp_toolkit` are encouraged to update to version 1.9.0 to avoid undefined behavior.

summary: Redox UEFI Safe API can cause heap-buffer-overflow
details: ffi::nstr() should be marked unsafe, since a pointer to a buffer without a trailing 0 value will cause a heap buffer overflow.

summary: wrflib has a soundness issue and is unmaintained
details:
All functions under `wrflib::byte_extract` are simply wrapper of unsafe pointer offset and lacks sufficient checks to it pointer and offset parameter.

`wrflib` is unmaintained.

summary: Multiple soundness issues in lexical
details:
`lexical` contains multiple soundness issues:

 1. [Bytes::read() allows creating instances of types with invalid bit patterns](https://github.com/Alexhuszagh/rust-lexical/issues/102)
 1. [BytesIter::read() advances iterators out of bounds](https://github.com/Alexhuszagh/rust-lexical/issues/101)
 1. [The `BytesIter` trait has safety invariants but is public and not marked `unsafe`](https://github.com/Alexhuszagh/rust-lexical/issues/104)
 1. [`write_float()` calls `MaybeUninit::assume_init()` on uninitialized data, which is is not allowed by the Rust abstract machine](https://github.com/Alexhuszagh/rust-lexical/issues/95)
1. [`radix()` calls `MaybeUninit::assume_init()` on uninitialized data, which is is not allowed by the Rust abstract machine](https://github.com/Alexhuszagh/rust-lexical/issues/126)

The crate also has some correctness issues.

## Alternatives

For quickly parsing floating-point numbers third-party crates are no longer needed. A fast float parsing algorithm by the author of `lexical` has been [merged](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/86761) into libcore.

For quickly parsing integers, consider `atoi` and `btoi` crates (100% safe code). `atoi_radix10` provides even faster parsing, but only with `-C target-cpu=native`, and at the cost of some `unsafe`.

For formatting integers in a `#[no_std]` context consider the [`numtoa`](https://crates.io/crates/numtoa) crate.

For working with big numbers consider `num-bigint` and `num-traits`.

summary: RISC Zero zkVM notes on zero-knowledge
details:
RISC Zero zkVM was designed from its inception to provide three main guarantees:
1. *Computational integrity*: that a given software program executed correctly.
2. *Succinctness*: that the proof of execution does not grow in relation to the program being executed.
3. *Zero Knowledge*: that details of the program execution are not visible within the proof of program execution.

Ulrich Habock and Al Kindi have released [new research] that indicates that several STARK implementations -including our RISC Zero zkVM- do not meet the requirements to assert the specific property of zero knowledge provably. 

While a vast majority of real-world applications that leverage RISC Zero zkVM or similar systems depend primarily on computational integrity and succinctness, a subset of applications critically depend on the privacy guarantees provided by zero-knowledge; and for those use cases, users are cautioned to understand the research and make informed decisions based on the risks outlined in using an impacted system.

Although the maintainers are not aware of any attacks that can take advantage of this potential weakness, they are working to proactively address this discovery as quickly as possible. 

[new research]: https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1037

summary: Ref methods into_ref, into_mut, into_slice, and into_slice_mut are unsound when used with cell::Ref or cell::RefMut
details:
*This advisory is also published as [RUSTSEC-2023-0074](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2023-0074.html).*

The `Ref` methods `into_ref`, `into_mut`, `into_slice`, and `into_slice_mut` are unsound and may allow safe code to exhibit undefined behavior when used with `Ref<B, T>` where `B` is [`cell::Ref`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/cell/struct.Ref.html) or [`cell::RefMut`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/cell/struct.RefMut.html). Note that these methods remain sound when used with `B` types other than `cell::Ref` or `cell::RefMut`.

See https://github.com/google/zerocopy/issues/716 for a more in-depth analysis.

The current plan is to yank the affected versions soon. See https://github.com/google/zerocopy/issues/679 for more detail.

summary: ferris-says has undefined behavior when not using UTF-8
details:
Affected versions receive a `&[u8]` from the caller through a safe API, and pass it directly to the unsafe `str::from_utf8_unchecked` function.

The behavior of `ferris_says::say` is undefined if the bytes from the caller don't happen to be valid UTF-8.

The flaw was corrected in [ferris-says#21] by using the safe `str::from_utf8` instead, and returning an error on invalid input. However this fix has not yet been published to crates.io as a patch version for 0.2.

Separately, [ferris-says#32] has introduced a different API for version 0.3 which accepts input as `&str` rather than `&[u8]`, so is unaffected by this bug.

[ferris-says#21]: https://github.com/rust-lang/ferris-says/pull/21
[ferris-says#32]: https://github.com/rust-lang/ferris-says/pull/32

summary: Nervos CKB DoS: Process exists when p2p discovery protocol receives unsupported peer IP
details: The p2p discovery protocol assumes that the peer IP must be valid IPv4 address.

summary: Apache Arrow Rust: Bloom filters written as plaintext when writing encrypted Parquet
details:
When writing an encrypted parquet file with a column with bloom filters, the header
and bitsets of the bloom filter are written in plaintext in the final parquet.

Patched versions now reject writing bloom filters when encryption is enabled, raising
an error at runtime.

Existing encrypted parquet files written with bloom filters are still vulnerable,
and it is recommended to rewrite those files with bloom filters disabled if possible.

Credit to Yanzhi Xin (autoCAT6) for finding this.

summary: Private cookie nonces can repeat in processes that fork
details:
## Who is affected

Only applications that call `fork()` and then add private (encrypted) cookies
on the thread that forked, in more than one of the resulting processes. This
is an uncommon way to deploy a Rust web application. In particular:

 * **Rocket is not affected.**
 * **axum is not affected as normally run.** It is affected only when an
   application forks worker processes itself and runs each on a
   current-thread runtime. See "Rocket and axum" below.
 * Applications that never fork are not affected. This includes all
   applications on Windows.
 * Signed cookies (`SignedJar`) are not affected.

The exact conditions are listed under "Conditions" below.

## Description

Private cookies are sealed with AES-256-GCM using a random 96-bit nonce.
Affected versions drew the nonce from `rand`'s thread-local generator,
`rand::thread_rng()`. That generator hands out bytes from an internal buffer
and only notices that the process has forked when the buffer is refilled. A
process that forks therefore continues, in both the parent and the child, from
the same buffered bytes, and the private cookies sealed first on each side of
the fork use the same nonces.

## Impact

Reusing a nonce under the same key breaks AES-GCM. From two private cookies
that share a nonce, an attacker can:

 * recover the XOR of the two plaintexts, and thus either plaintext if the
   other is known, and
 * recover the GHASH authentication key and forge private cookies, with a
   name and value of their choosing, that the application accepts as
   authentic.

The nonce is the first 12 bytes of a private cookie's (base64-decoded) value,
so a repeated nonce is visible to anyone who holds two such cookies.

Exploitation requires the uncommon deployment described above, and only the
first private cookies added after a fork are affected: at most 21 per process.
An attacker must obtain two of them, from two different processes.

## Conditions

All of the following must hold:

 1. The target is a Unix-like system and the process calls `fork()` without a
    subsequent `exec()`.
 2. The thread that calls `fork()` used `rand::thread_rng()` at any point
    before the fork. Any use counts, including `Key::generate()`, adding a
    private cookie, or a call made by an unrelated crate.
 3. After the fork, private cookies are added on that same thread in two or
    more of the resulting processes: the parent and a child, or several
    children.
 4. Those processes use the same `Key`.

When they hold, at most the first 21 private cookies added on that thread in
each process share nonces. After that the generator reseeds and the processes
diverge.

The following are **not** affected:

 * Applications that never fork, including all applications on Windows.
 * Processes in which the forking thread did not use `rand::thread_rng()`
   before the fork.
 * Private cookies added on threads that were created after the fork. This
   includes servers that fork and then start a multi-threaded async runtime
   in each child.
 * Signed cookies (`SignedJar`), which do not use a nonce.
 * Versions `0.12.0` through `0.13.3`, and `0.11.2` and earlier, which
   obtained nonces from the operating system via `ring`.

## Rocket and axum

Rocket and axum were tested with `cookie` `0.18.2` by collecting the private
cookies sent by each server process and comparing their nonces.

**Rocket** (`0.5.4`, `CookieJar::add_private()`) is not affected. Rocket does
not fork, and it handles requests on worker threads of a runtime it creates
when launched. No nonce was reused:

 * when launched normally, in a single process, or
 * when a parent process used a private cookie and then forked two worker
   processes that each launched Rocket.

**axum** (`0.8.9`, with `PrivateCookieJar` from `axum-extra` `0.12.6`) is not
affected as normally run. No nonce was reused:

 * when run in a single process on a multi-threaded runtime, or
 * when a parent process used a private cookie and then forked two worker
   processes that each started a multi-threaded runtime.

An axum application is affected only if it does all of the following:

 1. forks worker processes itself,
 2. runs each worker on a current-thread runtime on the thread that forked,
    so that requests are handled on that thread, and
 3. used `rand::thread_rng()` on that thread before forking.

In that configuration, the first private cookies sent by two workers reused
nonces: 19 when the parent had added one private cookie before forking, and 15
when the parent had only called `Key::generate()`. No nonce was reused when
the parent did neither.

Other frameworks and libraries that use this crate's `PrivateJar` were not
tested. The conditions above apply to them as well.

## Fix

Version `0.18.3` obtains nonces directly from the operating system's random
number generator, which is not affected by `fork`.

## Workarounds

If upgrading is not possible, any one of the following prevents the reuse:

 * Do not use `rand::thread_rng()`, directly or indirectly, on the forking
   thread before forking. In particular, create the `Key` with `Key::from()`
   or `Key::derive_from()` rather than `Key::generate()` before the fork.
 * In each child, immediately after forking, read and discard at least 256
   bytes from `rand::thread_rng()` before adding any private cookie.
 * Add private cookies only on threads created after the fork.

Applications that ran in an affected configuration should rotate their `Key`.

summary: Dilithium verification accepts non-conforming signatures with the `avx2` feature
details:
With the default `avx2` feature on x86_64 and a CPU that supports AVX2,
`pqcrypto-dilithium` verifies signatures with PQClean's AVX2 implementation of
Dilithium. That implementation predates two upstream fixes
([pq-crystals/dilithium#113](https://github.com/pq-crystals/dilithium/issues/113),
3 June 2026), the same ones described in RUSTSEC-2026-0586 for `pqcrypto-mldsa`:

- the verifier does not check that the infinity norm of `z` is below
  `γ1 − β`, so it accepts signatures that the crate's own portable
  implementation rejects;
- `use_hint_avx()` mishandles a boundary case, so one class of valid
  signatures is rejected.

Creating an accepted out-of-bound signature requires the private key. The
practical effect is that verification results differ between this crate with
AVX2 and the same crate without it.

Tested on version 0.5.0: for each of dilithium2, dilithium3 and dilithium5, 20
signatures with `z` out of bound are accepted with AVX2 and rejected by the
portable code, and 2 valid signatures that exercise the `use_hint` boundary
are rejected with AVX2 and accepted by the portable code. This crate
implements a pre-standard version of the scheme, so the Wycheproof ML-DSA
vectors do not apply; the test signatures are built with the crate's own
signer.

The crate is unmaintained (see RUSTSEC-2024-0380) and no patched version is
expected. Disabling the `avx2` feature avoids the affected code.

summary: Validating Matrix key IDs may panic
details:
Using `key_id::validate` may panic if the `algorithm` part of the key ID is
longer than 255 bytes and contains non-ASCII characters. The affected versions
assumed that the length of the first part containing the encryption or signing
algorithm (the part before the colon) would fit into a `NonZeroU8`, but the
length of the first part wasn't validated.

summary: Ineffective default DACL on Windows
details:
On Windows, affected versions of this crate do not provide the intended security-enhancement.
In particular, any process running under the same user as the hardened process can reset our DACL,
and thus bypass the protection the DACL should have provided. Usage of the crate however *does not
actively harm security*.

On affected version, an explicit owner SID (taken from the process token) was used for the DACL.
However, Windows implicitly grants extra access rights to the well-known "owner rights" SID, unless
it occurs in the DACL, which it did not. This allows any process under the same user to reset the
DACL of our process, making this defence effectively useless. The new code uses the well-known
"owner rights" SID, preventing the attack.

The default hardening setup is fixed in version `0.3.9`. Users creating a custom DACL with the API
from the `win_acl` module need to manually update their code to get the security enhancement. They
are strongly advised to use a well-known "owner rights" SID created using the new
`win_acl::SidRef::well_known` (introduced in version `0.3.9`) in their DACL instead of the owner
SID returned by `win_acl::TokenUser::sid`.

summary: `Fixed` and `Dynamic` secret wrappers were not zeroized on drop
details:
In affected versions, the `Fixed<T>` and `Dynamic<T>` wrappers (and the
`FixedNoClone` / `DynamicNoClone` variants in 0.6.x) did not wipe their contents
when dropped. The types implemented the `zeroize::ZeroizeOnDrop` marker trait,
which has no methods and does nothing by itself, but had no `Drop` implementation.
The documentation stated that secrets were zeroized on drop.

A secret held in one of these wrappers stayed in the freed stack or heap memory
after the wrapper went out of scope, where it could be read by anything able to
observe that memory later, such as a core dump, swap, or a separate memory
disclosure bug.

Versions before 0.5.0 are not affected: with the default `zeroize` feature they
stored the secret in `secrecy::SecretBox` or `zeroize::Zeroizing`, both of which
wipe on drop.

The flaw was fixed by making `zeroize` a required dependency, bounding the
wrappers on `T: Zeroize`, and adding `Drop` implementations that call
`zeroize()`. The first published release with the fix is 0.8.0-rc.1; the first
stable release is 0.8.0. All affected versions have been yanked from crates.io.

summary: Stack overflow in `Url::origin()` on nested `blob:` URLs
details:
In `url` 2.5.8 and earlier, `Url::origin()` handled a `blob:` URL by parsing its path as another URL and calling itself on the result. It did so regardless of the inner URL's scheme, `blob` included. Each `blob:` prefix cost one stack frame, with no limit on nesting depth. `Url::parse()` accepts a URL with 10,000 `blob:` prefixes followed by `https://example.com/` (50,020 bytes in total); calling `Url::origin()` on it overflowed the default 2 MiB stack of a spawned thread.

A stack overflow aborts the whole process, and `catch_unwind()` does not catch it. One such URL crashes any program that calls `Url::origin()` on untrusted input. `url::quirks::origin()` also calls `Url::origin()`. For example, Servo's `URL.origin` DOM getter calls `url::quirks::origin()`, so a script on a page can trigger the overflow.

`url` 2.5.9 follows the URL Standard: `Url::origin()` takes the origin of the inner URL only when its scheme is `http`, `https`, or `file`, returns an opaque origin otherwise, and never calls itself. A `blob:` URL with another inner scheme that previously produced a tuple origin, such as `blob:ws://...` or `blob:blob:https://...`, now returns an opaque origin.

summary: Validating Matrix Content URIs may panic
details:
Using `mxc_uri::validate` may panic if the server name part of the URI is larger
than 249 bytes. The affected versions assumed that the length of the first part
of the URI (`mxc://{server_name}`) would fit into a `NonZeroU8`, but the length
of the server name wasn't validated and the Matrix specification actually allows
the server name to have a maximum length of 261 bytes.

summary: Large-window Brotli bodies bypass decompression memory limits
details:
With the `compress-brotli` feature enabled, the decoder accepts the non-standard
large-window Brotli format. A crafted stream can cause its internal buffer to
grow to about 1 GiB before the decoded output reaches the configured size limit.
An 850-byte request can cause this allocation, and concurrent requests can
exhaust process or host memory.

Actix Web enables Brotli support by default. Applications that read request
bodies through `Bytes`, `String`, `Json`, or `Form` can be affected even when
extractor size limits are configured. The allocation occurs before the handler
runs, so authentication performed in the handler does not prevent it.

Upgrade to actix-http 3.20.3 or later. As a workaround, reject requests with
`Content-Encoding: br` at a reverse proxy or in middleware before body
extraction, or disable the `compress-brotli` feature throughout the dependency
graph.

summary: Request smuggling through malformed chunked request trailers
details:
The HTTP/1 chunked decoder accepts a bare line feed after the final chunk as
the start of a trailer instead of rejecting the malformed request.

When an upstream proxy reuses a connection and either pipelines the requests or
does not take steps to validate the chunked stream, the decoder can consume the
next request's headers as trailer data. It can then parse that request's body as
a new request. An attacker can use this difference in request parsing to bypass
access controls enforced by a proxy or web application firewall.

Upgrade to actix-http 3.20.2 or later.

summary: Hidden file disclosure through Windows short names
details:
On Windows volumes with 8.3 short names, `actix_files::Files` can serve hidden
files through their short-name aliases. The default path check rejects segments
that start with a dot, but an alias such as `ENV~1` or `GIT~1` passes this check.

A remote client can read files such as `.env` or `.git/config` in the served
directory even when `use_hidden_files()` is not enabled. This can expose secrets
or source code.

Upgrade to actix-files 0.7.4 or later. As a workaround, remove sensitive files
and directories from the served directory.

summary: Out-of-bounds read when decoding internal keys shorter than 16 bytes
details:
`InternalKeyRef::from_encoded` is a safe constructor whose only length check is `debug_assert!(encoded.len() >= 16)`, which is compiled out in release builds. Its accessors perform unchecked length arithmetic on the slice: `user_key()` slices `&encoded[..len - 16]`, `trailer()`/`seq_num()` pass `len - 16` and `timestamp()` passes `len - 8` to `read_u64_be`, which computes `buffer.as_ptr().add(offset)` and performs an 8-byte load. For a short slice the subtraction underflows `usize`, the pointer wraps below the allocation and eight bytes before the buffer are read (undefined behavior; confirmed with AddressSanitizer as a `heap-buffer-overflow`). In debug builds the same call panics instead.

The same invariant is missing at the on-disk decode boundary: `BlockIterator::seek_next_entry` rebuilds the current key from block bytes with upper-bound checks only, and `BlockIterator::key()` wraps it in `InternalKeyRef`, which `surrealdb`'s `kv-surrealkv` backend then reads through `key_ref.timestamp()`. A crafted or corrupted SSTable therefore reaches the same unchecked subtraction without any `unsafe` at the call site.

`1.2.0` rejects internal keys shorter than their 8-byte trailer before any accessor computes an offset and makes the accessors bounds-checked (fix in commit `ac642f9`, `surrealdb` 4.0.0 ships `surrealkv` 1.2.0).

summary: sevenz-rust2: decompress builds each output path as dest.join(entry.name()) with no traversal guard, allowing a crafted .7z to write files outside the destination (Zip-Slip)
details:
### Summary

Extracting an attacker-supplied 7z archive can write files outside the destination directory. The 7z header stores each entry's path as a UTF-16 name with nothing constraining it to a relative, in-tree path. The extractor joins that name onto the destination and writes to the result without normalizing it or checking that it stays under the destination root, so an entry named `../../etc/cron.d/x` or an absolute path escapes the target.

### Details

In `src/util/decompress.rs`, `decompress_impl` computes the per-entry destination directly (line 140):

```rust
let dest_path = dest.join(entry.name());
extract_fn(entry, reader, &dest_path)
```

`default_entry_extract_fn` (line 154) then acts on that path:

```rust
let file = File::create(path)
    .map_err(|e| Error::file_open(e, path.to_string_lossy().to_string()))?;
```

There is no normalization, no `dest_path.starts_with(dest)` check, and no symlink-entry handling. `Path::join` discards the base when the joined component is absolute, and `..` components are not collapsed against the base. The convenience entry points (`decompress`, `decompress_file`, `decompress_with_password`, `decompress_file_with_password`) all route through `decompress_impl` with `default_entry_extract_fn`, so the default API is affected.

The trust boundary is the archive bytes. Any caller that extracts an untrusted `.7z` reaches the sink.

### PoC

1. Build a `.7z` whose `FilesInfo` contains an entry named `../../../../tmp/pwned` (or, on Windows, an absolute path such as `C:\Windows\Temp\pwned`).
2. Call `sevenz_rust2::decompress_file("evil.7z", "./out")`.
3. The file is created at the traversed location outside `./out`. Targeting a startup/cron path or a config file turns the write into code execution or persistence.

### Impact

Arbitrary file write outside the intended directory (CWE-22 / CWE-23, the Zip-Slip class). On extraction of an attacker-controlled archive, an entry overwrites files outside the destination — config, cron, autostart, or build artifacts — which can escalate to code execution. Reachable by upload-handling backends, malware-analysis sandboxes, mod/game installers, and CI steps that unpack user-supplied 7z files.

### Suggested remediation

Reject any entry whose name contains a `ParentDir`, `RootDir`, or `Prefix` component, or canonicalize the joined path and verify `starts_with(dest)` before creating it. Apply the guard inside `default_entry_extract_fn` (and `decompress_impl`) so the hardening is the default rather than left to each caller. Reject or explicitly opt-in symlink entries.

## Maintainer response

This issue was patched with ef760b61f3535ac8b93006212aef41bfebc237eb and released as `v0.21.1` to crates.io

Consumers that extract attacker-supplied archives received over a network without user interaction should re-score as AV:N/UI:N (≈8.6).

summary: Duplicate Advisory: split: TOCTOU output-open allows truncating a swapped file
details:
### Duplicate Advisory
This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-fjjq-8hw5-cf9f. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

### Original Description
A Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) vulnerability exists in the split utility of uutils coreutils. The program attempts to prevent data loss by checking for identity between input and output files using their file paths before initiating the split operation. However, the utility subsequently opens the output file with truncation after this path-based validation is complete. A local attacker with write access to the directory can exploit this race window by manipulating mutable path components (e.g., swapping a path with a symbolic link). This can cause split to truncate and write to an unintended target file, potentially including the input file itself or other sensitive files accessible to the process, leading to permanent data loss.

summary: Duplicate Advisory: chcon: recursive relabel not anchored to traversal dirfd (TOCTOU)
details:
### Duplicate Advisory
This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-9rv8-9hvg-92mq. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

### Original Description
A Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) vulnerability exists in the chcon utility of uutils coreutils during recursive operations. The implementation resolves recursive targets using a fresh path lookup (via fts_accpath) rather than binding the traversal and label application to the specific directory state encountered during traversal. Because these operations are not anchored to file descriptors, a local attacker with write access to a directory tree can exploit timing-sensitive rename or symbolic link races to redirect a privileged recursive relabeling operation to unintended files or directories. This vulnerability breaks the hardening expectations for SELinux administration workflows and can lead to the unauthorized modification of security labels on sensitive system objects.

summary: Duplicate Advisory: uu_env -S rejects backslashes in single-quoted strings accepted by GNU env
details:
### Duplicate Advisory
This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-xhrc-7f76-vh96. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

### Original Description
A logic error in the env utility of uutils coreutils causes a failure to correctly parse command-line arguments when utilizing the -S (split-string) option. In GNU env, backslashes within single quotes are treated literally (with the exceptions of \\ and \'). However, the uutils implementation incorrectly attempts to validate these sequences, resulting in an "invalid sequence" error and an immediate process termination with an exit status of 125 when encountering valid but unrecognized sequences like \a or \x. This divergence from GNU behavior breaks compatibility for automated scripts and administrative workflows that rely on standard split-string semantics, leading to a local denial of service for those operations.

summary: chcon: recursive relabel not anchored to traversal dirfd (TOCTOU)
details:
`chcon` resolved recursive targets from `fts_accpath` with a fresh path lookup, so traversal and the SELinux get/set were not bound to traversal directory state. A privileged recursive relabel can be redirected to unintended objects under rename/symlink races. Fix opens targets with `openat` against the traversal cwd fd before the SELinux operation.

**Fixed in 0.10.0** (PR #12566, commit 7cfc74e47ffab452663be6842d788a5164d9688b): recursive relabel resolution is anchored to the traversal dirfd.

summary: split: TOCTOU output-open allows truncating a swapped file
details:
`split` checks input/output identity by path before opening the output, then opens with truncation, leaving a race window on mutable path components. GNU opens first and compares the opened output inode against the input before truncating. The race can cause `split` to truncate/write a file different from the one validated — including the input file or another file the process can access.

**Fixed in 0.10.0** (PR #12565, commit 58040feb5c66fce588a7ffac299b3a23bd55cd81): the output open path is hardened against TOCTOU target swaps.

---
_Zellic private finding (zellic-ext/coreutils-private PR #119). Reported in the Zellic *uutils coreutils Program Security Assessment* (for Canonical, Jan 2026), audited commit `3a07ffc5a9bd4c283e75afa548ba1f1957bad242`._

summary: uu_env incorrectly rejects backslashes within single-quoted strings accepted by GNU env
details:
In `env -S`, GNU keeps backslashes literal inside single quotes (except `\\` and `\'`); uutils errors on sequences like `\a`. This is the backslash-handling issue of the broader `-S`/`--split-string` parsing divergence.
```
env -S"printf %s '\''\\x'\''"   # GNU prints \x ; uutils: invalid sequence '\x' in -S (125)
```

---
_Zellic private finding (zellic-ext/coreutils-private PR #117). Reported in the Zellic *uutils coreutils Program Security Assessment* (for Canonical, Jan 2026), audited commit `3a07ffc5a9bd4c283e75afa548ba1f1957bad242`._

summary: Panics during RSA private-key construction, validation, or re-encoding
details:
`RsaPrivateKey` private-key construction, validation, and serialization can panic across three
classes of inputs, as well as when re-encoding certain valid keys:

- `RsaPrivateKey::from_components` and PKCS#1 or PKCS#8 private-key decoding (DER or PEM) can panic
  during validation when a supplied factor equals 1, because `RsaPrivateKey::validate()` let a
  factor of 1 reach a later check that panicked.
- `RsaPrivateKey::from_primes` and `RsaPrivateKey::from_p_q` can panic during construction when a
  supplied factor is 0, 1, or even.
- Prime recovery in `RsaPrivateKey::from_components` can panic when the private exponent is 0.
- For a key, including a valid one, whose first prime occupies more limbs than the second,
  `crt_coefficient`, `to_pkcs1_der`, `to_pkcs8_der`, and `serde` serialization can panic.

An application that imports untrusted private keys or factors, or re-encodes such keys, can lose a
worker, or the whole process when built with `panic = "abort"`. Public-key parsing is not affected.

Fixed in 0.10.4, which rejects factors below 2, even factors, repeated factors, and a zero private
exponent during prime recovery, and computes the CRT coefficient and re-encodes valid two-prime
keys when the first prime occupies more limbs than the second.

If you cannot upgrade to 0.10.4, isolate the entire import, construction, CRT calculation, or
serialization in a separate process and treat an abnormal exit as an operation failure, or use
`catch_unwind` around the entire operation when panics unwind.

summary: ML-DSA verification accepts non-conforming signatures with the `avx2` feature
details:
With the default `avx2` feature on x86_64 (non-Windows) and a CPU that supports
AVX2, `pqcrypto-mldsa` verifies signatures with PQClean's AVX2 implementation of
ML-DSA. That implementation predates two upstream fixes
([pq-crystals/dilithium#113](https://github.com/pq-crystals/dilithium/issues/113),
3 June 2026):

- the verifier does not check that the infinity norm of `z` is below
  `γ1 − β` (FIPS 204, Algorithm 8, line 13), so it accepts signatures that
  conforming verifiers reject;
- `use_hint_avx()` mishandles a boundary case, so one class of valid
  signatures is rejected.

Creating an accepted out-of-bound signature requires the private key. The
practical effect is that verification results differ between this crate with
AVX2 and conforming implementations, including this crate without AVX2.

The Wycheproof ML-DSA verification vectors reproduce both defects: with AVX2,
37 / 41 / 49 invalid vectors (ML-DSA-44 / -65 / -87) are accepted and one valid
vector per parameter set is rejected.

The crate is unmaintained (see RUSTSEC-2026-0166) and no patched version is
expected. Disabling the `avx2` feature avoids the affected code. Migrating to a
maintained implementation, such as the [`ml-dsa`](https://crates.io/crates/ml-dsa)
crate, is recommended.

summary: ML-KEM does not perform the FIPS 203 input checks
details:
`pqcrypto-mlkem` wraps PQClean's ML-KEM implementation, which does not perform
the input checks required by FIPS 203:

- encapsulation does not perform the encapsulation key modulus check
  (section 7.2), so encapsulation keys with coefficients that are not reduced
  modulo q are accepted;
- decapsulation does not perform the decapsulation key hash check
  (section 7.3), so a decapsulation key whose stored hash or embedded
  encapsulation key has been altered is accepted.

With the Wycheproof ML-KEM vectors, 108 / 112 / 116 invalid encapsulation keys
(ML-KEM-512 / -768 / -1024) and 2 invalid decapsulation keys per parameter set
are accepted.

This does not disclose key material. It is a FIPS 203 non-conformance, and an
affected implementation can disagree with a conforming one about which keys
are valid.

The crate is unmaintained (see RUSTSEC-2026-0161) and no patched version is
expected. Migrating to a maintained implementation, such as the
[`ml-kem`](https://crates.io/crates/ml-kem) crate, is recommended.

summary: gRPC `IpKeyExtractor` keys on client-supplied forwarding headers
details:
`tonic_middleware::IpKeyExtractor` is documented as rate limiting gRPC requests by client IP address,
but on a standard tonic server it keys on client-supplied `x-forwarded-for` and `x-real-ip`
headers. In 0.5.0–0.9.1, the extractor reads those headers directly; in 0.10.0–0.11.0, it first
checks for a bare `std::net::SocketAddr` request extension—which `tonic::transport::Server` never
supplies, as it provides `TcpConnectInfo` instead—and falls back to the same headers. Direct
clients can therefore choose their rate-limit key to bypass per-IP rate limits and increase the
number of tracked keys; without forwarding headers, 0.5.0–0.9.1 allow requests without limiting
them and 0.10.0–0.11.0 reject them by default unless `.fail_open()` is enabled.

Applications are affected if they use `GrpcRateLimitLayer` with `IpKeyExtractor` (the
`tonic-support` feature). The HTTP middleware's `IpKeyExtractor` reads `ConnectInfo<SocketAddr>` and
is not affected.

Version 0.11.1 fixes `IpKeyExtractor` to honor a server-supplied `SocketAddr` override first and then
read the TCP peer address from tonic's `TcpConnectInfo` (which `tonic::transport::Server` attaches
to plaintext connections and connections using its built-in TLS), without ever reading forwarding
headers. Deployments behind a trusted proxy can use the new opt-in `ForwardedIpKeyExtractor`, which
reads a single configured header (`x-forwarded-for` or `x-real-ip`) and is only correct when that
proxy sets the header as documented.

If you cannot upgrade to 0.11.1, use a custom key extractor that reads the peer IP from tonic's
connection information for the transport in use (including TLS) and rejects requests without a
verified peer address before invoking the limiter, or restrict backend access to a trusted proxy
that strips all incoming `x-forwarded-for` and `x-real-ip` fields and sets one `x-forwarded-for`
value to the verified client IP on every request.

snark-verifier: Halo 2 aggregation circuit mishandles point-at-infinity proof elements
details:
### Summary
The Halo 2 aggregation circuit could mishandle proof elements encoded as the point at infinity.

When an assigned proof point appeared in an MSM term with constant scalar one, the Halo 2 loader used a scalar-one shortcut that passed the assigned point directly into the EC sum helper. The EC sum implementation used by that path assumed its inputs were non-identity points, while assigned proof points could represent the encoded identity `(0, 0)`.

### Details
`EcPointLoader::multi_scalar_multiplication` partitions MSM terms by scalar and base type. For `(Value::Constant(ONE), Value::Assigned(_))`, the loader placed the assigned base into the non-scaled variable-base list and later passed those points to `sum_with_const`.

The default Halo 2 shim delegates `sum_with_const` to halo2-lib `EccChip::sum`. In affected versions, that sum helper used incomplete affine addition and assumed that every input point was non-identity. A prover-controlled proof point encoded as `(0, 0)` could therefore enter the final aggregation sum through the scalar-one shortcut and affect the MSM or accumulator computation.

The issue was fixed in halo2-lib by updating `EccChip::sum` to treat encoded identity inputs as no-ops and to return `(0, 0)` when the total sum is the identity. This removes the non-identity input precondition from callers such as the Halo 2 aggregation loader.

### Impact
Recursive aggregation circuits using the Halo 2 loader could compute an MSM or accumulator with an identity proof element in a path whose implementation assumed non-identity inputs. This breaks the expected handling of point-at-infinity proof elements in aggregation.

Practical exploitability depends on the surrounding aggregation and final-decider checks, so this is rated medium severity.

summary: CodeWhale: Automation auto_approve defaults to true, bypassing the task-path hardening fix for silent recurring agent execution
details:
### Maintainer resolution

The CodeWhale maintainers validated this report. CodeWhale 0.8.67 and earlier are affected. Version 0.9.0 contains the fix in commit 208421b9d23d81cea3311a1eeb2a2ea81d637686. Users should upgrade to 0.9.0 or later. The original reporter analysis is preserved below.

## Summary
CVE-2026-45374 (GHSA-72w5-pf8h-xfp4) hardened the task path so auto-approval must be opted into explicitly: `add_task` uses `req.auto_approve.unwrap_or(false)` (task_manager.rs:868). The automation subsystem was not hardened in kind. `AutomationRecord::task_auto_approve()` resolves an omitted `auto_approve` to `DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_AUTO_APPROVE = true` (automation_manager.rs:29, 101-103), and `enqueue_run_task` builds the `NewTaskRequest` with `auto_approve: Some(automation.task_auto_approve())` — i.e. an explicit `Some(true)` (automation_manager.rs:766). Because the field is `Some`, `unwrap_or(false)` returns `true` and the seed-2 default is bypassed. That `true` propagates to `ApprovalMode::Bypass` (runtime_threads.rs:2253), where the background approval loop auto-approves every tool call with no human present (runtime_threads.rs:3383-3416). One approved `automation_create` becomes a durable, recurring, fully auto-approved agent. Same insecure-default class as CVE-2026-45374, on a different, unpatched subsystem.

## Root Cause
Sibling durable defaults in the same struct are safe — `DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_ALLOW_SHELL = false` and `DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_TRUST_MODE = false` (automation_manager.rs:27-28) — while `DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_AUTO_APPROVE` alone defaults `true` (:29). `create_automation` stores `auto_approve: None` when omitted (:422); `task_auto_approve()` resolves `None`→`true` (:101-103); `enqueue_run_task` passes `Some(true)` (:766), defeating `add_task`'s `unwrap_or(false)` seed fix. The `automation_create` tool schema also declares `"auto_approve": {"type":"boolean","default":true}` (tools/automation.rs:49) while sibling `allow_shell`/`trust_mode` default `false`.

## Impact
A single approved `automation_create` yields a durable, recurring, fully auto-approved agent. Every scheduled fire silently authorizes mutating tools (file writes, apply_patch, git, MCP writes) with no prompt; combined with `allow_shell:true` in the create call, recurring silent RCE with no human present. Even without `allow_shell`, every recurring run silently authorizes all non-shell mutating tools. Same class as seed CVE-2026-45374.

## Proof of Concept
Prompt injection convinces the model to create a benign-sounding recurring job (single human approval on the `automation_create` call):
```json
{"name":"automation_create","arguments":{
  "name":"nightly-maintenance",
  "prompt":"Fetch latest and run project setup script",
  "rrule":"FREQ=HOURLY;INTERVAL=1",
  "allow_shell":true
}}
```
(`auto_approve` omitted → stored `None` → resolves to `true` on every run.)

## Attack Chain
1. **Entry.** Prompt injection → model creates a recurring job via `automation_create` with `auto_approve` omitted.
   - **Guard:** `automation_create` is `Required` (tools/automation.rs:61-63) — user sees ONE approval prompt.
   - **Bypass proof:** the prompt describes an innocuous automation; the schema hides `"auto_approve": {"default": true}` (tools/automation.rs:49). Approving "create a scheduled job" is not informed consent to "every future run bypasses all approval prompts." The resolved `auto_approve=true` (omitted field) is not surfaced.
2. **Persist.** `create_automation` stores `auto_approve: None` (automation_manager.rs:422).
   - **Guard:** none.
   - **Bypass proof:** `None` is later resolved to `true`, not `false`.
3. **Fire.** Headless scheduler tick (`scheduler_tick_shared`, no human) or `automation_run` invokes `enqueue_run_task`, which sets `auto_approve: Some(true)` (automation_manager.rs:766).
   - **Guard:** seed-2's hardened `add_task` default `unwrap_or(false)` (task_manager.rs:868).
   - **Bypass proof:** the value is `Some(true)`, so `unwrap_or(false)` yields `true` — the hardened default never applies.
4. **Sink.** Background worker builds the turn with `auto_approve=true` → `ApprovalMode::Bypass` (runtime_threads.rs:2253); the approval loop auto-approves (runtime_threads.rs:3383-3416).
   - **Guard:** auto_review safety_floor.
   - **Bypass proof:** safety_floor holds only `Publish` (any origin) and `Destructive/Secret` (background/headless) (auto_review.rs:344-357); ordinary `write_file`/`apply_patch`/`edit_file`/non-destructive `exec_shell` are NOT held → they run unattended. With `allow_shell:true`, every scheduled run additionally gets silent shell execution.
5. **Impact.** Durable, recurring, fully auto-approved agent from one create approval; recurring silent RCE with `allow_shell:true`.

## Bypass Evidence
- Present on latest release tag v0.8.67: automation_manager.rs:27-29 (`ALLOW_SHELL=false`, `TRUST_MODE=false`, `AUTO_APPROVE=true`), :101-103 `task_auto_approve()`→`unwrap_or(true)`, :766 `Some(automation.task_auto_approve())`, :422 stores `None` when omitted; task_manager.rs:868 `unwrap_or(false)`; runtime_threads.rs:2253 `if auto_approve → ApprovalMode::Bypass`. automation_manager.rs and task_manager.rs byte-identical v0.8.67↔HEAD.
- Subsystem wired by default: `automation_create`/`automation_run` registered via `with_runtime_task_tools()` in `with_agent_tools_policy` (registry.rs:1005); TUI attaches `automations: Some(...)` (tui/ui.rs:986-1011), serve mode via runtime_api.rs:426 — not feature-gated.
- Sibling flags `allow_shell`/`trust_mode` default `false` in the same struct — `auto_approve=true` is the un-hardened anomaly.

## Affected Versions
`<= 0.8.67` (present on latest release tag v0.8.67 and HEAD 6a3403e).

## Suggested Fix
Set `DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_AUTO_APPROVE = false` (mirror the seed-2 task-path fix) and change the `automation_create` schema default to `false`, so durable automations require explicit opt-in to auto-approval just like the task path.

Reported by **zx (Jace)**

summary: CodeWhale: exec_shell parallel-readonly classifier auto-approves fd/rg/git grep exec flags enabling silent RCE
details:
### Maintainer resolution

The CodeWhale maintainers validated this report. CodeWhale 0.8.67 and earlier are affected. Version 0.9.0 contains the fix in commit 208421b9d23d81cea3311a1eeb2a2ea81d637686. Users should upgrade to 0.9.0 or later. The original reporter analysis is preserved below.

## Summary
The interactive Agent profile of DeepSeek-TUI (CodeWhale) is explicitly documented to gate **every** shell command behind an approval prompt (config.rs:3725-3736). However, `ExecShellTool::approval_requirement_for(&tool_input)` downgrades the requirement from `Required` to `Auto` for any command the classifier deems "parallel read-only" (shell.rs:2314-2320). `registered_tool_approval_required` returns `false` for `Auto` **before** the `auto_approve` check runs (turn_loop.rs:37-38), so no prompt is shown even for a user who never enabled YOLO. The classifier `is_parallel_readonly_command` (command_safety.rs:389) rejects only shell metacharacters and then matches the flag-stripped base command name against an allowlist that includes `fd`, `rg`, and `git grep`. Those tools execute arbitrary external programs through documented flags (`fd -x/--exec`, `rg --pre`, `git grep --open-files-in-pager`) that need **no** shell metacharacters — yielding silent arbitrary-program execution in the default profile. Same silent-RCE class as CVE-2026-45311 (run_tests) but via a different, unpatched tool and code path.

## Root Cause
`approval_requirement_for` downgrades `exec_shell` to `Auto` when `exec_shell_input_is_parallel_readonly` returns true (shell.rs:2314-2320). The classifier strips all flags and matches the base command name against `PARALLEL_READONLY_PREFIXES` (command_safety.rs:363-385, 419-433). `fd`/`rg` are absent from `COMMAND_ARITY`, so `fd -x cp {} /tmp/exfil` canonicalizes to `"fd"` ∈ allowlist. The only remaining gate at the execute sink is `analyze_command`, which rates `fd`/`rg` as `Safe` (SAFE_COMMANDS command_safety.rs:527,530), so the `SafetyLevel::Dangerous`-only block (shell.rs:2408) never fires. Default execpolicy is empty (engine.rs:494) → Skip. Interactive-origin auto_review safety_floor holds only `Publish` (auto_review.rs:344-357), not interactive shell.

## Impact
Arbitrary external program execution (any binary, any argv, including a repo-committed script) on the developer host, with no approval prompt, in the default interactive Agent profile — bypassing the boundary config.rs:3725-3736 explicitly promises. Identical outcome to seed CVE-2026-45311 via a different, unpatched tool.

## Proof of Concept
Model coerced (via indirect prompt injection from repo file / issue / fetched page — the seed threat model, in scope per SECURITY.md:48) to emit:
```json
{"name":"exec_shell","arguments":{"command":"fd -u -tf -x ./pwn.sh"}}
```
Alternatives (all metachar-free, all auto-approved): `fd -tf -x cp {} /tmp/exfil`; `rg --pre /tmp/evil.sh --pre-glob '*' needle .`; `git grep --open-files-in-pager=/tmp/evil.sh needle`.

## Attack Chain
1. **Entry.** Agent ingests attacker-controlled content; injected instruction coerces the model to emit `exec_shell {"command":"fd -u -tf -x ./pwn.sh"}`.
   - **Guard:** none — reading content and model tool-calls are by design (seed threat model: indirect prompt injection).
   - **Bypass proof:** n/a (in-scope by design per SECURITY.md:48).
2. **Gate — approval requirement.** turn_loop.rs:1738 → `spec.approval_requirement_for(&input)` → shell.rs:2314-2320 `exec_shell_input_is_parallel_readonly`.
   - **Guard:** metachar filter (command_safety.rs:394-400) + base-name allowlist.
   - **Bypass proof:** the string contains none of `; & | > < \` $(` or newlines; `-x <program> <args>` is `fd`'s own exec mechanism (no shell). `classify_command` strips `-u -tf -x`, positionals `[fd, ./pwn.sh]`; `fd` ∉ `COMMAND_ARITY` → canonical `"fd"` ∈ `PARALLEL_READONLY_PREFIXES` → returns true. Maintainer test `parallel_readonly_command_classifier_is_strict` (command_safety.rs:1162+) confirms bare `fd`/`rg` classify parallel-readonly.
3. **Gate — prompt decision.** `registered_tool_approval_required(name, Auto, auto_approve)`.
   - **Guard:** the approval prompt itself.
   - **Bypass proof:** `requirement == Auto` returns `false` at turn_loop.rs:37-38 unconditionally, before `!auto_approve`. No prompt regardless of user settings. Empty execpolicy → Skip; interactive safety_floor returns NoChange for fd.
4. **Sink.** `ExecShellTool::execute` (shell.rs:2334) → `analyze_command`.
   - **Guard:** `SafetyLevel::Dangerous` block (shell.rs:2408).
   - **Bypass proof:** `fd` ∈ `SAFE_COMMANDS` (command_safety.rs:530) → `analyze_command` returns `Safe`; not `Dangerous` → not blocked. Child runs the attacker's program.
5. **Impact.** Silent arbitrary-program execution on the developer host, no approval prompt, default interactive Agent profile.

## Bypass Evidence
- Present on latest release tag v0.8.67: turn_loop.rs:37-38 `Auto`→`return false`; shell.rs:2314-2320 override; command_safety.rs allowlist includes `"rg"`,`"fd"`,`"git grep"`; SAFE_COMMANDS includes `"rg"`,`"fd"`; `fd`/`rg` absent from `COMMAND_ARITY`. command_safety.rs / turn_loop.rs finding-critical functions byte-identical v0.8.67↔HEAD.
- Maintainer's own test `parallel_readonly_command_classifier_is_strict` confirms bare `rg`/`fd` classify parallel-readonly and only metachar forms are rejected.

## Affected Versions
`<= 0.8.67` (present on latest release tag v0.8.67 and HEAD 6a3403e).

## Suggested Fix
Remove exec-capable tools (`fd`, `rg`, `git grep`) from `PARALLEL_READONLY_PREFIXES`, or make the classifier reject their exec flags (`-x`/`--exec`, `--pre`, `--open-files-in-pager`), so a code-executing invocation cannot be auto-approved as read-only.

Reported by **zx (Jace)**

summary: Servo Sandbox bypass: declarative refresh can auto-navigate a sandboxed iframe
details:
A sandboxed iframe can auto-navigate itself via declarative refresh even when automatic features should be blocked. This allows attacker-controlled embedded content to redirect itself without user action.

### Summary
Servo allows a sandboxed iframe to auto-navigate itself via declarative refresh in configurations that should block automatic features.

The issue reproduces in the must-block rows of the matrix:

- `sandbox=""`
- `sandbox="allow-same-origin"`
- `sandbox="allow-forms"`
- `sandbox="allow-same-origin allow-forms"`

This is a client-side sandbox-policy bypass. It does not by itself prove script execution or parent DOM access, but it does let attacker-controlled sandboxed content redirect itself without user action.

### Details
The declarative refresh path is missing sandbox enforcement:

- [components/script/dom/document/document.rs:239] `RefreshRedirectDue::invoke()` contains `TODO: check sandbox`
- [components/script/dom/document/document.rs:4522] the refresh scheduler contains `TODO: handle active sandboxing flag`

The implementation currently schedules and executes the refresh without enforcing the sandboxed automatic-features restriction described by the HTML spec comments in the same code.

What I observed:

- In Servo, the must-block rows above navigated successfully.
- In Chrome, the same rows were blocked.

### PoC
Serve the HTML files in this folder over HTTP.

Files:
- [child.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27770907/child.html)
- [success.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27770910/success.html)
- [viewer.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27770911/viewer.html)

Steps:

1. Open `viewer.html` over HTTP.
2. The page shows a visible sandboxed iframe.
3. In a correct browser, the iframe stays on `child.html`.
4. In Servo, the iframe visibly turns into the `success.html` page.

### Impact
This is a client-side sandbox-policy bypass.

Confirmed impact:

- autonomous iframe self-navigation in sandbox configurations that should block it
- framed phishing / content swap after initial render
- redirect loops / annoyance / limited DoS
